record.title: A structured pipeline cut false positive grading of research level mathematical proofs, but generality remains untested
record.summary: The Ramanujan Challenge authors report an AI-assisted workflow for reviewing research-level mathematical submissions in natural language, computer algebra and Lean. It executes submitted Python under a fixed environment, has separate agents summarize the proof and code, compares those summaries, then presents the result to a human reviewer. Against one-shot Claude Opus 5 judgments on the same challenge set, the authors report that false 'Correct' verdicts fell from 23.4% to 5.8% for 137 natural-language proofs and from 38.3% to 3.3% for 120 CAS/Lean artifacts. Agreement with one human evaluator rose from 65.7% to 66.4% for proofs and from 45.8% to 58.3% for code. The paper says each artifact was reviewed by one human without cross-checking; participants self-selected and reported their tools. These are one paper's results, not independent confirmation of generality or reduced expert workload.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a workflow that executes submitted Python under a fixed environment, separately summarizes natural-language proofs and code with AI agents, compares the summaries, and presents them to a human reviewer.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors' Ramanujan Challenge evaluation, false-positive Correct verdicts by Claude Opus 5 fell from 23.4% (32 of 137) to 5.8% (8 of 137) for natural-language proofs and from 38.3% (46 of 120) to 3.3% (4 of 120) for CAS/Lean artifacts when using the pipeline rather than one-shot prompting. Agreement with the single human evaluator changed from 65.7% to 66.4% for proofs and from 45.8% to 58.3% for code.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report one correct and complete Lean-formalized proof of one published conjecture among the evaluated submissions; they state the conjecture solutions were not yet fully evaluated and one remained open.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish independent reproduction, agreement with multiple blinded expert evaluators, reduced real-world expert workload, or transfer of the measured grading changes to other models, mathematical problems, or scientific domains.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reanalysis or replication with multiple blinded expert evaluators was inspected. The single-human reference may contain errors or evaluator-specific bias, as the authors acknowledge.
The reported effect is limited to one self-selected number-theory challenge and one Claude Opus 5 comparison; transfer to other models, proof domains or scientific claims is not established.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported effect transfers, reducing false acceptance of incomplete research-level proofs could improve the throughput and reliability of AI-for-mathematics evaluation and later AI-for-science work. The evidence is a single author-reported challenge dataset with one human evaluator per artifact, so its consequence is notable but not yet a field-wide shift.
limitations: The quantitative results are reported by the paper's authors and were not reproduced in this activation.
Each artifact's reference assessment came from one human evaluator without cross-checking; the authors identify potential error and evaluator-background bias.
Participants self-selected and tools were self-reported; participation varied from one to all ten problems.

Proof-level agreement with the human evaluator increased only from 65.7% to 66.4%, even as false-positive 'Correct' judgments declined. The work does not establish reduced expert time or generality beyond this challenge.
The reported Lean-formalized conjecture proof is paper-reported; this activation did not inspect its source or verify its theorem statement and dependencies.
brief.summary: The Ramanujan Challenge authors report an AI-assisted workflow for reviewing research-level mathematical submissions in natural language, computer algebra and Lean. It executes submitted Python under a fixed environment, has separate agents summarize the proof and code, compares those summaries, then presents the result to a human reviewer. Against one-shot Claude Opus 5 judgments on the same challenge set, the authors report that false 'Correct' verdicts fell from 23.4% to 5.8% for 137 natural-language proofs and from 38.3% to 3.3% for 120 CAS/Lean artifacts. Agreement with one human evaluator rose from 65.7% to 66.4% for proofs and from 45.8% to 58.3% for code. The paper says each artifact was reviewed by one human without cross-checking; participants self-selected and reported their tools. These are one paper's results, not independent confirmation of generality or reduced expert workload.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report fewer false Correct classifications and improved agreement with a single human reference evaluator in the challenge-specific comparison. The paper also reports one correct and complete Lean formalization of a published conjecture, while noting that conjecture submissions had not yet been fully evaluated.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv v1 page contains the workflow, tables, dataset counts and stated limitations. This activation did not reproduce the grading comparison, inspect supplemental submission-level data, or independently verify the formalized proof.
technical.mechanism: The workflow first executes submitted Python scripts and collects deterministic behavior/code-structure summaries. GPT 5.6-Sol separately summarizes natural-language proof files; Claude Opus 5 separately summarizes CAS/Lean artifacts; GPT 5.6-Sol compares the summaries for agreements, conflicts and shared issues. A human evaluator sees those materials. The comparison uses Claude Opus 5 for both one-shot and pipeline-assisted verdicts.
technical.regime: A single author-run evaluation of submissions to the Ramanujan Challenge, held July–August 2026 with 8 questions and 2 conjectures. The paper reports 137 graded natural-language proofs and 120 CAS/Lean artifacts in the comparison. Submitters self-selected and self-reported tools; one human evaluator assessed each artifact without cross-checking.
technical.strongest_baseline: Claude Opus 5 with one-shot prompting is compared with the same model using the workflow, against the human evaluator's verdicts as reference labels. Proof agreement moved from 65.7% to 66.4%, while false acceptance fell from 23.4% to 5.8%. CAS/Lean agreement rose from 45.8% to 58.3%, while false acceptance fell from 38.3% to 3.3%. The paper's single-reviewer uncertainty also applies to reference labels.

brief.title: A structured pipeline cut false positive grading of research level mathematical proofs, but generality remains untested
brief.why_it_matters: When AI-generated scientific claims arrive faster than experts can check them, false acceptance can become a bottleneck. This study reports that separating proof and code analysis and comparing their summaries reduced one model's false 'Correct' verdicts on a research-level mathematics challenge. The modest change in proof agreement, the single-evaluator reference labels, and the narrow challenge set make this a promising evaluation method to test, not evidence that AI can yet verify research proofs reliably across domains.
